theorem.statement:
For every \(I=(M,a,X,Y,c,L,B)\in\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{exp}}\) whose underlying undirected full graph \(G\) has exactly one simple cycle \(K\), the two-arc reachability augmentation specified by \(\operatorname{UnicycleHandle}\) gives a sound-and-complete polynomial-size certificate calculus and an exact polynomial-time algorithm. More explicitly, there is at most one directed edge \(e^\star\) of \(K\) for which the complementary arc \(K\setminus\{e^\star\}\) is a directed path from the tail of \(e^\star\) to its head. Every Beckers witness has a cost-nonincreasing normalization consisting of an alternate assignment \(w\in R(U\cup V)\), one support row \(\rho_Z\in R(\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z))\) for each \(Z\in V\setminus\{X\}\), the row-difference deletion set
\[
D^0(w,\rho)=\{p\to Z:Z\ne X,\ \rho_{Z,p}\ne w_p\},
\]
and, only if deleting \(e^\star\) would leave its whole complementary arc retained, one additional cycle edge. Conversely, every normalized tuple satisfying the local actual-row hitting tests and the support conditions \(w_Z\in A_Z(\rho_Z)\) is a Beckers witness. Hence the minimum witness cost, with value \(+\infty\) when no witness exists, is the minimum of at most \(2|E(K)|-1\) explicitly specified min-sum programs on a factor graph of cycle rank one. Cutting its unique factor-graph cycle, conditioning on one boundary value, and applying the displayed min-sum recurrences in the proof computes this minimum using \(O(L^7)\) arithmetic and address operations; every finite rational encountered has \(O(B+\log(L+1))\) bits. The algorithm returns either a positive witness and an exact optimum certificate or polynomial-size infeasibility tables constituting a separating cut. In particular, the full-unicycle class is decidable in polynomial time.
theorem.proof_tex:
Write \(D_H=E(G)\setminus E(H)\). By the canonical replay lemma, a feasible causal witness is equivalently a retained graph \(H\in\mathcal H(G)\), the local equalities
\[
Q_Z^{\operatorname{Pa}_H(Z)}(a_{\operatorname{Pa}_H(Z)})=\{a_Z\}
\qquad(Z\in V),                                           \tag{1}
\]
and an assignment \(w\in R(U\cup V)\) such that
\[
w_U=a_U,\qquad w_X\ne a_X,\qquad w_Y\ne a_Y,
\qquad
w_Z\in Q_Z^{\operatorname{Pa}_H(Z)}(w_{\operatorname{Pa}_H(Z)})
\quad(Z\in V\setminus\{X\}).                            \tag{2}
\]
The equation at \(X\) is absent in (2) because the alternate model intervenes on \(X\). Since \(X\) is a singleton event and \(X\ne Y\), its usual minimality requirement has no nonempty proper subevent. Thus (1)--(2), together with graphical legality, characterize the causal query rather than define it.

We first determine graphical legality on a unicycle. Let \(e=p\to Z\) be a deleted edge. If the undirected edge underlying \(e\) does not lie on \(K\), any second undirected path between \(p\) and \(Z\) would form another undirected cycle. Hence no retained directed path from \(p\) to \(Z\) exists. If \(e\) lies on \(K\), its only possible alternative undirected path is \(K\setminus\{e\}\). Therefore
\[
p\leadsto_H Z
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
K\setminus\{e\}\text{ is oriented from \(p\) to \(Z\) and every edge of it is retained}.       \tag{3}
\]
There is at most one edge with the orientation property in (3). Indeed, list the edges in one cyclic order and give an edge sign \(+\) when it follows that order and \(-\) otherwise. An edge has a directed complementary path from its tail to its head exactly when its sign is opposite to every other sign. Two such exceptional edges would force a third edge, which exists because a simple cycle has length at least three, to have both opposite signs. This is impossible. Call the exceptional edge \(e^\star\) when it exists. It follows directly from the definition of a Beckers-legal retained graph and (3) that every subgraph is legal when \(e^\star\) does not exist, while, when it does exist,
\[
H\in\mathcal H(G)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
e^\star\notin D_H
\ \text{or}\ 
D_H\cap\bigl(E(K)\setminus\{e^\star\}\bigr)\ne\varnothing.                                  \tag{4}
\]
The two bits in (4), namely whether the shortcut is retained and whether its complementary directed arc has been broken, are exactly the two-arc reachability signature required by \(\operatorname{UnicycleHandle}\).

We next prove the normalization, including its cost claim. Fix any witness \((H,w)\) satisfying (1)--(2). For every \(Z\ne X\), the definition of the projected table and (2) provide a row \(\rho_Z\in R(\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z))\) such that
\[
w_Z\in A_Z(\rho_Z),
\qquad
\rho_Z|_{\operatorname{Pa}_H(Z)}=w|_{\operatorname{Pa}_H(Z)}.                                  \tag{5}
\]
Define
\[
D^0=\{p\to Z\in E(G):Z\ne X,\ \rho_{Z,p}\ne w_p\}.                                           \tag{6}
\]
Equation (5) implies \(D^0\subseteq D_H\): an edge whose parent coordinate differs in (5) cannot be retained. If \(D^0\) is legal, set \(D=D^0\). If it is illegal, (4) implies
\[
e^\star\in D^0,
\qquad
D^0\cap(E(K)\setminus\{e^\star\})=\varnothing.                                                \tag{7}
\]
Since \(D_H\) is legal and contains \(D^0\), (4) supplies an edge
\[
f\in D_H\cap(E(K)\setminus\{e^\star\}).                                                       \tag{8}
\]
In this case set \(D=D^0\cup\{f\}\). In both cases \(D\subseteq D_H\), and (4) proves that \(G\setminus D\) is legal.

Let
\[
S_Z(D)=\{p\in\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z):p\to Z\notin D\}.
\]
Because \(D\subseteq D_H\), one has \(S_Z(D)\supseteq\operatorname{Pa}_H(Z)\). Equality (1) and the local hitting equivalence show that \(\operatorname{Pa}_H(Z)\) hits every member of \(\mathcal B_Z\). Its superset \(S_Z(D)\) therefore does also, so the same lemma gives
\[
Q_Z^{S_Z(D)}(a_{S_Z(D)})=\{a_Z\}
\qquad(Z\in V).                                                                                \tag{9}
\]
For \(Z\ne X\), every retained parent in \(S_Z(D)\) agrees between \(\rho_Z\) and \(w\), by (6). The possibly additional deleted edge \(f\) only removes a matching constraint. Thus (5) and the definition of projection give
\[
w_Z\in A_Z(\rho_Z)
\subseteq Q_Z^{S_Z(D)}(w_{S_Z(D)}).                                                             \tag{10}
\]
Equations (4), (9), and (10), followed by the canonical replay lemma, prove that \((G\setminus D,w)\) is a witness. Nonnegativity of every edge cost yields
\[
\sum_{e\in D}c(e)\le \sum_{e\in D_H}c(e),                                                     \tag{11}
\]
because \(D\subseteq D_H\). Notice that deleting an incoming edge of \(X\) cannot be a row-difference deletion because no structural row is used at the intervened node; such an edge survives normalization unless it is the single edge \(f\) required by (8).

Conversely, suppose \(w\), the rows \(\rho_Z\), and a set \(D\) have the displayed normalized form, obey (4), satisfy \(w_U=a_U\), \(w_X\ne a_X\), \(w_Y\ne a_Y\), and satisfy
\[
w_Z\in A_Z(\rho_Z)\quad(Z\ne X),
\qquad
S_Z(D)\cap\Delta\ne\varnothing
\quad(Z\in V,\ \Delta\in\mathcal B_Z).                                                      \tag{12}
\]
The second part of (12) and the local hitting equivalence imply (9); the first part and the definition of \(D^0\) imply (10). Condition (4) supplies graphical legality. Canonical replay then makes \(G\setminus D\) a legal structural simplification, and (10) makes the already complete assignment \(w\) a solution after intervening on \(X\). Since \(w_Y\ne a_Y\), this is a Beckers witness. This proves both directions of the normalized-certificate characterization. Finiteness of all domains implies that the minimum of (11) is attained whenever a witness exists.

It remains to give the promised computable minimum. For a support row \(\rho_Z\), put
\[
\delta^0_{p\to Z}(\rho,w)=\mathbf 1\{\rho_{Z,p}\ne w_p\}\quad(Z\ne X),
\qquad
\delta^0_{p\to X}=0.                                                                           \tag{13}
\]
If \(e^\star\) is absent, use one unconstrained mode. If \(e^\star\) exists, use the following \(2|E(K)|-1\) modes:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{mode \(0\):}&\delta^0_{e^\star}=0;\\
\text{mode \(g\), for \(g\in E(K)\setminus\{e^\star\}\):}
  &\delta^0_{e^\star}=\delta^0_g=1;\\
\text{repair mode \(\bar f\), for \(f\in E(K)\setminus\{e^\star\}\):}
  &\delta^0_{e^\star}=1\text{ and }\delta^0_h=0
    \text{ for every \(h\in E(K)\setminus\{e^\star\}\), with \(f\) additionally deleted.}
\end{array}                                                                                     \tag{14}
\]
Modes \(0\) and \(g\) cover every legal base set \(D^0\); the repair modes cover exactly (7)--(8). Although a legal base set with several deleted complementary edges can occur in more than one mode \(g\), duplication does not alter a minimum.

For a mode \(b\), let \(f_b=f\) in repair mode \(\bar f\), and let \(f_b=\bot\) otherwise. Given the values of \(Z\) and all its parents, define the local potential
\[
\Phi_Z^b(w_Z,w_{\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z)})
=
\min_{\tau}
\left\{
  \sum_{p:p\to Z\in D_Z^b(\tau,w)}c(p\to Z)
\right\},                                                                                       \tag{15}
\]
where \(\tau=\rho_Z\in R(\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z))\) and \(w_Z\in A_Z(\rho_Z)\) when \(Z\ne X\), whereas \(\tau=\star\) is the sole choice when \(Z=X\). The deleted incoming set in (15) is
\[
D_Z^b(\tau,w)
=
\{p\to Z:Z\ne X,\ \rho_{Z,p}\ne w_p\}
\cup
\{f_b:f_b=p\to Z\text{ for some \(p\)}\}.                                                     \tag{16}
\]
The minimum in (15) is subject to the conjuncts of (14) concerning edges entering \(Z\) and to
\[
\bigl(\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z)\setminus\{p:p\to Z\in D_Z^b(\tau,w)\}\bigr)
\cap\Delta\ne\varnothing
\qquad(\Delta\in\mathcal B_Z).                                                                \tag{17}
\]
It is \(+\infty\) if no \(\tau\) satisfies these conditions. Each restriction in (14) is unary in an edge indicator, so assigning its conjunct to the factor at the edge's head is exact.

For each vertex \(q\in U\cup V\), define a unary feasibility cost \(\psi_q\) by
\[
\psi_q(v)=
\begin{cases}
0,&q\in U\text{ and }v=a_q,\\
0,&q=X\text{ and }v\ne a_X,\\
0,&q=Y\text{ and }v\ne a_Y,\\
0,&q\in V\setminus\{X,Y\},\\
+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}                                                                                     \tag{18}
\]
Let \(C^\star\) be the minimum deletion cost among causal witnesses, with the empty minimum defined as \(+\infty\). The normalization already proved shows, without defining the causal target to be this program, that \(C^\star\) satisfies the identifying equality
\[
C^\star
=
\min_b\ \min_{w\in R(U\cup V)}
\left\{
  \sum_{Z\in V}\Phi_Z^b(w_Z,w_{\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z)})
  +\sum_{q\in U\cup V}\psi_q(w_q)
\right\}.                                                                                       \tag{19}
\]
Indeed, (5)--(11) map every causal witness to a feasible term of no larger cost in (19), while (12) maps every finite term of (19) to a causal witness of exactly that term's cost. Hence neither inequality in (19) is assumed.

For completeness, we now solve (19) explicitly. Form a bipartite factor graph with a variable vertex for each \(q\in U\cup V\), a factor vertex for each \(Z\in V\), and edges joining the factor \(Z\) to \(Z\) and to every member of \(\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z)\). Contracting every factor--child edge recovers the underlying undirected graph of \(G\), so contraction preserves the cycle rank and the factor graph has cycle rank one. Choose a variable vertex \(q_0\) on its unique cycle, condition on one \(v\in R(q_0)\), and delete that variable vertex after substituting \(v\) into every incident factor. What remains is a forest.

On each rooted component of this forest use the recurrences
\[
m_{q\to Z}(x_q)
=
\psi_q(x_q)+
\sum_{T\in N(q)\setminus\{Z\}}m_{T\to q}(x_q),                                                  \tag{20}
\]
and
\[
m_{Z\to q}(x_q)
=
\min_{x_{N(Z)\setminus\{q\}}}
\left\{
\Phi_Z^b(x_{N(Z)})+
\sum_{r\in N(Z)\setminus\{q\}}m_{r\to Z}(x_r)
\right\}.                                                                                       \tag{21}
\]
Here a conditioned occurrence of \(q_0\) is replaced by \(v\), and an empty sum is zero. An induction from the leaves proves that every message equals the minimum total potential in the component on its sending side, conditional on the displayed boundary value: the leaf case is (20) or (21) with an empty sum, and removing the receiving edge makes the remaining sending-side components disjoint, so adding their already-minimized costs and then minimizing their boundary values gives the induction step. Consequently, summing the component minima, adding \(\psi_{q_0}(v)\), minimizing over \(v\in R(q_0)\), and finally minimizing over the modes in (14) gives exactly (19).

All tables in (15) are explicitly computable. A deliberately coarse bound suffices: there are at most \(L\) modes and factors; a factor has at most \(L^2\) assignments of its output and parent tuple, at most \(L\) candidate support rows for each assignment, and at most \(L^2\) explicitly indexed bad-row coordinate incidences to scan for (17). Thus construction of all local tables and evaluation of (20)--(21) use \(O(L^7)\) arithmetic and address operations. Each finite number is a sum of a subset of the input edge costs. A common denominator has binary length at most the sum of the input denominator lengths, and summing at most \(L\) numerators adds at most \(\lceil\log_2(L+1)\rceil\) bits. Hence every finite message has \(O(B+\log(L+1))\) bits, and exact addition, comparison, and budget comparison have polynomial bit complexity.

A finite optimum records its mode, conditioned boundary value, minimizing choices in (20)--(21), assignment \(w\), rows \(\rho_Z\), and optional repair edge \(f\). Equations (4), (12), and the displayed rows verify the positive witness directly. Supplying all message arrays for all modes lets a verifier rescan every minimum in (20)--(21); these arrays lower-bound every feasible term of (19), while the recorded witness attains their final minimum, so they certify optimality. If every mode has value \(+\infty\), the sets of finite entries in the same message arrays are closed under every feasible local extension in (20)--(21) but exclude every accepting conditioned root state. They therefore form a polynomial-size separating cut, and rescanning the recurrences verifies infeasibility.

As an exact smallest check, consider \(U\to X\to Y\) together with \(U\to Y\), with binary variables, actual zeros, \(X=U\), and \(Y=X\wedge U\). Here \(e^\star=U\to Y\). Producing \(w_X=w_Y=1\) requires the support row \((U,X)=(1,1)\) at \(Y\), so \(D^0=\{U\to Y\}\), which is illegal. Repair by deleting \(U\to X\) makes the actual projection of \(X=U\) contain \(1\), violating (9); repair by deleting \(X\to Y\) makes the parent-free actual projection of \(Y\) contain the output \(1\) from row \((1,1)\), again violating (9). Thus every repair mode is rejected, exactly as full graphical legality requires. This also confirms that the reachability signature cannot be discarded even though the endogenous graph is a chain. The construction and recurrence above prove the positive polynomial-time side of the open question.
